source_text: V. Post hanc vero sententiam turba fratrum dicebat: Et nos cum ipso decollemur. propter hoc tumultus fratrum exortus est et multa turba eum prosecuta est. et ita idem Cyprianus in agrum Sexti productus est et ibi se lacerna byrro exspoliavit et genu in terra flexit et in orationem se domino prostravit. et cum se dalmatica exspoliasset et diaconibus tradidisset, in linea stetit et coepit spiculatorem sustinere. cum venisset autem spiculator, iussit suis ut eidem spiculatori viginti quinque aureos darent. linteamina vero et manualia a fratribus ante eum mittebantur. postea vero beatus Cyprianus manu sua oculos sibi texit. qui cum lacinias manuales ligare sibi non potuisset, Iulianus presbyter et Iulianus subdiaconus ei ligaverunt. ita beatus Cyprianus passus est, eiusque corpus propter gentilium curiositatem in proximo positum est. inde per noctem sublatum cum cereis et scolacibus ad areas Macrobii Candidiani procuratoris, quae sunt in via Mappaliensi, iuxta piscinas, cum voto et triumpho magno deductum est. post paucos autem dies Galerius Maximus proconsul decessit.
pass_a_gloss: After this sentence indeed the crowd of the brothers kept saying: Let us also be beheaded with him. On account of this a commotion of the brothers arose and a great crowd followed him. And so the same Cyprian was led out into the estate of Sextus and there stripped himself of hooded cloak and overcoat and bent knee on earth and threw himself down to the Lord in prayer. And when he had stripped off his dalmatic and handed it to the deacons, he stood in a linen garment and began to await the executioner. When the executioner had come, he ordered his people to give to that same executioner twenty-five gold pieces. Linen cloths and handkerchiefs were being spread before him by the brothers. Afterwards the blessed Cyprian covered his own eyes with his own hand. And since he could not tie the ends of the handkerchief for himself, Julian the presbyter and Julian the subdeacon tied them for him. Thus the blessed Cyprian suffered, and his body was laid nearby because of the curiosity of the pagans. Thence taken up by night with candles and torches it was conducted with great vow and triumph to the grounds of Macrobius Candidianus the procurator, which lie on the Mappalian road beside the fishponds. After a few days, however, Galerius Maximus the proconsul died.
pass_b_english: After this sentence was pronounced, the multitude of the brethren cried out, Let us also be beheaded with him.
A great stir arose among the brethren over this, and a large crowd followed him out.
And so Cyprian was brought into the field of Sextus, and there he stripped off his hooded cloak and outer mantle, and bent his knee upon the ground, and cast himself down before the Lord in prayer.
Then, having removed his dalmatic and given it to the deacons, he remained standing in his linen undergarment and began to wait for the executioner.
When the executioner arrived, Cyprian ordered his attendants to give that same executioner twenty-five gold pieces.
The brethren spread linen cloths and handkerchiefs before him.
Then blessed Cyprian covered his eyes with his own hand, and because he could not fasten the ends of the handkerchief for himself, Julian the presbyter and Julian the subdeacon fastened them for him.
In this way blessed Cyprian suffered martyrdom, and his body was laid in a place nearby because of the prying curiosity of the pagans.

From there it was taken up by night with candles and torches and borne with great devotion and triumphant rejoicing to the estate of Macrobius Candidianus the procurator, which lies on the Mappalian Way beside the fishponds.
A few days afterward Galerius Maximus the proconsul died.

choices.english: he stood in his linen undergarment
choices.why: ablative of garment after stripped of outer layers; context is remaining white tunic before the stroke
nocturnal funeral procession context; scolacibus is late spelling for faculae, torches

choices.english: with great prayer and triumphant rejoicing
choices.why: votum here is devout acclamation by Christians, paired with triumphus as martyr victory, not a mere wish
